column1: Late Starts, Re-starts, Zero Downloading & Incremental Downloading (Gap-Fill)
column41:
+*Prerequisites:*+

# Once a message is successfully sent on Kafka, the {{lLastActivityReference}} for that message should be recorded against the exchange/segment and count should be incremented. Essentially the {{lLastActivityReference}} of the last successful message should be stored for each exchange/segment
# This data is simultaneously persisted, or an ability should be developed to retrieve this information (from Kafka) on demand. 
# When the Client communicator + Adapter starts, the persisted data should be loaded back into memory
# During BOD, the data ({{lLastActivityReference}} & count) is reset to 0



+*Gap-fill scenarios (Triggers):*+

# Client Communicator + Adapter DLL is started late 
## Here there are no records already sent via Kafka, {{lLastActivityReference=0}}
## The gap-fill process should work here without modification
# Client Communicator + Adapter DLL went down and up
## Here there are some records already sent via Kafka, {{lLastActivityReference}}=N
## As long as {{lLastActivityReference}} is persisted, N should be available to us when we restart our component.
## Considering this, the gap-fill should work here without modification
# Interactive component crashed / restarted / exchange re-login
## Here header, data and trailer messages are received. Receiving the header should start live-data queuing, and the trailer should start gap-fill
## The gap-fill process should work here with some modification 



+*Gap-fill process:*+

# There are 2 triggers (events) in the gap-fill process, beginQueuing() and gapFill() while drainQueue() is the final act. The 3 activities are depicted as functions here for simplicity in understanding, the actual code may differ.
# In the above gap-fill scenarios, beginQueuing() and gapFill() will happen one after the other while in the 3rd scenario, beginQueuing() will happen when zero downloading header is received, while gapFill() will happen after the trailer is received.
## It is assumed that when we receive the trailer, all the gap entries are present in the database, otherwise it may result in data loss.
# When beginQueuing() starts, all live data will be sent to the queue instead of downstream (Kafka / GNL)
## This may be achieved by using a switch bQueueLiveMessages (atomic boolean) at the live data flow path to decide if the order should be sent downstream or the queue, this will be disabled by default, indicating the messages should be sent downstream.
## beginQueuing() will enable bQueueLiveMessages to start redirecting messages to the queue
# When gapFill() starts, all records after the {{lLastActivityReference}} will be fetched from the database and sent downstream.
## It is important to ensure that {{lLastActivityReference}} gets updated when each message is successfully sent to keep {{lLastActivityReference}} accurate
# When drainQueue() starts, all messages in the queue will be sent downstream, while more live messages pile up.
## Once the queue is empty, bQueueLiveMessages should be turned off to resume direct processing of live messages
## It is vital to _synchronize_ checking for empty queue and turning off bQueueLiveMessages to ensure that no additional messages get queued after we check if the queue is empty to avoid potential system defects.



+*Avoiding duplicates during download:*+

# When we extract messages from the DB for gap-fill, it may contain additional live messages from events occuring during gap-fill process.
# We process these messages along with actual ‘historical’ messages without concern, as long as our {{lLastActivityReference}} value gets updated correctly at all times.
# This way, when we drain the queue, some of the live messages being queued up during gap-fill and which were already processed as part of gap-fill from DB will be dropped before sending downstream, as the message {{lLastActivityReference}}< stored {{lLastActivityReference}}. 
# This check has to be present at all times before actually sending the data downstream to avoid duplication from these scenarios and otherwise.



Added “IsEnableGNL” in INI for Gnexlayer gap fill downloading.

column1: Low latency design strategies
column41:
h3. A) Bleeding-edge (bypass)

* NIC: ConnectX-6/7 (single-port) on a dedicated NUMA node.
* Stack: *Onload* or *VMA* or pure *DPDK*.
* Threads: 1 per RX queue, *busy-poll loop*, SCHED_FIFO, pinned to isolated cores.
* Book build: 1–2 threads per venue/symbol-bucket, on same NUMA, consuming SPSC rings.
* Expectation: *single-digit µs* wire→user, sub-20µs to applied-book if parsing is lean.

h3. B) Near-bypass (AF_XDP)

* AF_XDP (zero-copy), 1 RX queue per UMEM, *userspace polling*.
* Same pinning/NUMA/isolcpus setup.
* Expectation: *low-teens µs* wire→user with tight loops.

h3. C) Kernel sockets tuned

* UDP sockets + {{SO_BUSY_POLL}}, {{recvmmsg(VLEN=1..2)}}, RSS to dedicated queues.
* Turn off GRO/LRO, set IRQ affinities away from ingest cores, moderate ring sizes.
* Expectation: high-teens to a few dozen µs; very stable with careful tuning.

column1: Measuring and controlling jitter
column41:
* *Timestamp at the NIC*
** Use PTP-synced hardware timestamps. Subtract from user-space clock (converted via PHC/clock correction) to get *true wire→buffer* latency.
* *Track drops & queue depth*
** Poll {{ethtool -S}} counters. Drops on RX rings or in driver indicate you need more headroom or different pacing.
* *Latency histograms*
** Maintain *p50/p99/p99.9* for: wire→user, user→normalized update, normalized→book applied. Keep each stage under budget.
* *Backpressure*
** If strategies can’t keep up, *shed work upstream* (filter symbols/venues) rather than letting queues grow (which explodes tail latency).

column1: NIC and Kernel Settings
column41:
* *Offloads*
** *Disable LRO/GRO* (adds latency, reorders); keep checksum offload as needed.
* *RSS / flow steering*
** Enable RSS for UDP and program the *indirection table* so your target multicast flows land on your chosen queues.
** If the NIC supports *ntuple/flow-director*, add exact rules for multicast groups/ports.
* *Busy polling*
** {{/proc/sys/net/core/busy_poll}}, {{/proc/sys/net/core/busy_read}} tuned to small µs values; or per-socket {{SO_BUSY_POLL}}.
* *Socket buffers*
** Large {{SO_RCVBUF}} prevents transient drops but increases latency if you let queues build; with busy-polling and no drops, keep buffers moderate.
* *Timestamping*
** Enable *hardware timestamping* (PHC/PTP). Use it to measure wire-to-user latency and regress on changes.

column1: Hardware & Topology
column41:
* *NIC → NUMA locality*
** Place your ingest thread *on the NUMA node of the NIC* (check {{lspci -vv}}, {{numactl -H}}). Allocate all hot buffers on that node.
* *Cores & isolation*
** Isolate with kernel params: {{isolcpus=nohz,domain,managed_irq}} + {{nohz_full}} cores for your polling threads.
** *Pin threads* ({{sched_setaffinity}}) and use {{SCHED_FIFO}} high priority. Avoid siblings if Hyper-Threading is on; or disable HT for those cores.
* *Power & clocks*
** Disable deep C-states, set {{intel_pstate=disable}} (or equivalent), lock a high, fixed P-state. Disable Turbo if it introduces jitter on your platform.
* *Interrupt moderation*
** For polling designs: *disable interrupt moderation* entirely; ensure IRQs are not firing on your cores.
* *Queues*
** *One RX queue per polling thread*. Don’t share queues across threads.
** Right-size RX rings: too small → drops; too large → latency tail (queueing in hardware). Start ~512–1024 and measure tail.
** {color:#00b8d9}Match ring size to NSE TBT UDP packet size?{color}

column1: Masking of PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in applications
column41:
*“Identify and classify sensitive and Personally Identifiable Information (PII) data and apply measures for encrypting such data in transit and at rest.”*

That means:

* *At Rest* → When PII is stored in databases, servers, files, or backups, it should be encrypted.
* *In Transit* → When PII is transmitted (e.g., over APIs, email, file transfer), it should also be encrypted using secure protocols (TLS/SSL, VPN, etc.).

So, the circular makes *encryption of PII data mandatory* as part of cyber security best practices.

 

…………………………….

Masking of *PII (Personally Identifiable Information)* in applications is a *recommended cybersecurity practice* and is implied under the *data protection and breach prevention measures* in this circular.

Here’s how it works:

* The circular explicitly requires *encryption of PII in transit and at rest*.
* In addition, from a *practical security & compliance perspective*, *masking* (showing only partial data to users, e.g., r***@gmail.com or XXXX1234) is considered a *best practice* to prevent misuse or leakage of sensitive data in applications.
* Masking reduces exposure in *UI displays, logs, reports, and APIs* — so that even if a system is accessed by unauthorized users, the full PII isn’t visible.

summarizes our analysis of the latency issue reported by the upstream yesterday, specifically focusing on the example Order ID 30903003901295D1. We have compared the TCPDUMP packet capture with the GreekSoft logs and have identified two significant time gaps within our system that account for the high latency. The total delay identified for this order is approximately 4.723 seconds, which is unacceptable for DMA (Direct Market Access) orders.

 

*The full list of Order IDs that experienced high latency is as follows:*

|Cancel |1002.232499 |30903001546363F2|

|New    |4.888468 |30903003901309D1|
|Cancel    |4.887978 |30903003895944F2|

 

 

*Key findings*
Our investigation highlights the following time discrepancies, which are the root cause of the latency:

* *Packet-to-Application Lag*: There is a delay of approximately 2.840 seconds from the time the packet is received by the NIC (Network Interface Card) until it is logged by the GreekSoft application.
** NIC capture: 15:19:30.400238 (IST)
** GreekSoft log: 20250904-09:49:33.241 (GMT)
** Calculation: 15:19:30.400238 (IST) is equivalent to 09:49:30.400238 (GMT). The log time of 09:49:33.241 (GMT) shows a delay of ~2.840 seconds (33.241 - 30.400).
* *Confirmation-to-Send Lag*: The GreekSoft application took an additional 1.883 seconds to process the order confirmation and send the response back upstream.
** Response from exchange: 09:49:33.242 (GMT) (based on application's receipt)
** Application sends response: 09:49:35.125 (GMT)
** TCPDUMP captures response sent: 15:19:35.239052 (IST), which confirms the application's send time (09:49:35.239 GMT) is consistent with the GreekSoft log, indicating a significant delay after receiving the exchange confirmation.

*Impact on DMA orders*
DMA trading relies on fast execution, where every millisecond counts. A cumulative delay of over 4.7 seconds is highly detrimental to trading performance and can result in missed opportunities and potentially significant financial losses.

column1: Kafka Communication Structures & Details
column41:
*Kafka Message Flow :*

*Flow Overview*

# *MOSL will consume messages* from the topic: greek-order-req-dev.
#* This means MOSL reads incoming requests from this topic.
# *MOSL will produce messages* to the topic: greek-order-resp-dev.
#* This means MOSL sends out responses to this topic.

 

*Topic Naming Convention (Nomenclature)*

Each Kafka topic name is built using these parts:

* *Vendor Identifier:* greek
* *Message Identifier:* order or trade
* *Request/Response Identifier:* req (for requests) or resp (for responses)
* *Environment Identifier:* dev, uat, or prod

*Format:*
<vendor>-<msg>-<req/resp>-<env>

+*Note*+: all identifiers in the small case.

 

*Example Topic Names:*

* For an order request in dev: greek-order-req-dev
* For an order response in dev: greek-order-resp-dev
* For a trade request in prod: greek-trade-req-prod
* For a trade response in uat: greek-trade-resp-uat

 

*Kafka Partition Mapping*

To distribute load, each server reads/writes to a specific partition:



|*Sr No.*|*ServerId*|*Kafka Partition*|
|1|Server-1|0|
|2|Server-2|1|
|3|Server-3|2|

 

*Example 1: Order Topic Partition*

Suppose you are working with the *order request topic* in the *dev* environment:

* Topic: greek-order-req-dev

 

|*Topic Name*|*ServerId*|*Partition*|*Example Message Action*|
|greek-order-req-dev|Server-1|0|Greek Server-1 produces order requests|
|greek-order-req-dev|Server-2|1|Greek Server-2 produces order requests|
|greek-order-req-dev|Server-3|2|Greek Server-3 produces order requests|
|greek- order -resp-dev|Server-1|0|Greek Server-1 consumes order requests|
|greek- order -resp-dev|Server-2|1|Greek Server-2 consumes order requests|
|greek- order -resp-dev|Server-3|2|Greek Server-3 consumes order requests|



+*Message Topics (UAT) Update [22.09.2025]:*+

* Make sure {{CLOUD_DOMAIN}}, {{DOCS_DOMAIN}}, and {{ldap.CLOUD_DOMAIN}} point to your server IP.
* Open:
** {{https://<CLOUD_DOMAIN>}} → Nextcloud login page
** {{https://<DOCS_DOMAIN>}} → ONLYOFFICE welcome page
** {{https://ldap.<CLOUD_DOMAIN>}} → phpLDAPadmin login
* Certificates should be valid (Let’s Encrypt).

----

h3. ✅ *Step 3: Nextcloud Initial Admin*

Login with:

* *Username:* {{NC_ADMIN_USER}} (from {{.env}})
* *Password:* {{NC_ADMIN_PASS}}

Go to *Settings → Apps*:

* Check *Approval* app is enabled.
* Check *Workflow Engine* app is enabled.
* Check *ONLYOFFICE* app is enabled.
* Check *LDAP Integration* app is enabled.

----

h3. ✅ *Step 4: ONLYOFFICE Integration*

In Nextcloud:

* Go to *Settings → ONLYOFFICE*.
* Document Server URL should be {{https://<DOCS_DOMAIN>}}.
* JWT secret should match {{.env}} ({{OO_JWT_SECRET}}).
* Click *Save* and then *Open test document* → Should open in ONLYOFFICE editor.

----

h3. ✅ *Step 5: LDAP Integration*

* Go to *phpLDAPadmin* ({{https://ldap.<CLOUD_DOMAIN>}}), login as:
** {{cn=admin,<LDAP_BASE_DN>}}
** Password from {{.env}} ({{LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD}})
* Check groups exist: {{Editors}}, {{Reviewers}}, {{Approvers}}, {{ComplianceAdmins}}.
* In Nextcloud *Settings → LDAP/AD Integration*:
** Connection status should be *green*.
** Click *Detect Base DN* and *Test Login*.

----

h3. ✅ *Step 6: System Tags for ISO Workflow*

Run inside the Nextcloud container:

{noformat}docker exec -it nextcloud bash -c "php occ system:tag:list"
{noformat}

You should see:

* Draft
* In Review
* Approved
* Obsolete

----

h3. ✅ *Step 7: Approval App*

* Upload any file in Nextcloud.
* Select file → open *Approval* sidebar.
* You should see *Request approval* option.

----

h3. ✅ *Step 8: Flow Workflow*

* Go to *Settings → Flow*.
* You should see the *Workflow Engine* active.
* Create this rule (1 min manual step):
** *When:* File is tagged “In Review”
** *Then:* Send an approval request to *Approvers* group
** Add *then on approve → tag Approved*
** Add *then on reject → tag Draft*

_(If you want this automated via API, I can give you the script later.)_

----

h3. ✅ *Step 9: Test End-to-End*

# Login as *Editor* (LDAP user in {{Editors}} group).
# Create a document → tag *Draft*.
# Change tag to *In Review*.
# Login as *Approver* → see *Approval request*.
# Approve → tag changes to *Approved*.

Following is a *turn-key, self-hosted* stack with:

* *Nextcloud* (PHP-FPM) + *Nginx* (app server)
* *ONLYOFFICE Document Server*
* *MariaDB* + *Redis*
* *Traefik* reverse proxy with *automatic Let’s Encrypt TLS*
* *OpenLDAP* (with bootstrap groups) + *phpLDAPadmin*
* *Nextcloud auto-provisioning* script that:
** completes initial install,
** enables *ONLYOFFICE*, *Approval*, *Workflow Engine*, *LDAP*, *Automated Tagging*, *System Tags*,
** configures *ONLYOFFICE* (with JWT),
** creates *ISO doc control tags* (Draft / In Review / Approved / Obsolete),
** *(best-effort)* wires basic flows via available CLI; where Flow UI steps are still required, the script leaves everything pre-created and gives you a 1-minute finish in the UI.

{quote}Replace domains, passwords, and emails before running.{quote}

----

h1. 1) {{.env}} (put next to docker-compose.yml)

{noformat}# --- Domains & TLS ---
CLOUD_DOMAIN=cloud.example.com
DOCS_DOMAIN=docs.example.com
ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com

# --- Nextcloud Admin ---
NC_ADMIN_USER=admin
NC_ADMIN_PASS=ChangeThisAdminPass!

# --- DB ---
MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=ChangeThisRoot!
MYSQL_DATABASE=nextcloud
MYSQL_USER=nextcloud
MYSQL_PASSWORD=ChangeThisDB!

# --- ONLYOFFICE ---
OO_JWT_SECRET=ChangeThisOOJWT!

# --- LDAP (OpenLDAP bootstrap) ---
LDAP_ORG=Example Inc
LDAP_DOMAIN=example.com
LDAP_BASE_DN=dc=example,dc=com
LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=ChangeThisLDAP!
LDAP_READONLY_USER_PASSWORD=ChangeThisRO!

# --- Networks ---

h1. 2) {{docker-compose.yml}}

{noformat}version: "3.9"

volumes:
  db_data:
  nextcloud_data:
  nextcloud_apps:
  nextcloud_config:
  nextcloud_custom:
  redis_data:
  onlyoffice_data:
  traefik_letsencrypt:
  ldap_data:
  ldap_config:

networks:
  proxy:
    external: false
  internal:
    external: false

services:
  traefik:
    image: traefik:v3.0
    container_name: traefik
    restart: unless-stopped
    command:
      - --api.dashboard=false
      - --providers.docker=true
      - --providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false
      - --entrypoints.web.address=:${TRAEFIK_HTTP_PORT}
      - --entrypoints.websecure.address=:${TRAEFIK_HTTPS_PORT}
      - --certificatesresolvers.le.acme.email=${ADMIN_EMAIL}
      - --certificatesresolvers.le.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json
      - --certificatesresolvers.le.acme.httpchallenge=true
      - --certificatesresolvers.le.acme.httpchallenge.entrypoint=web
    ports:
      - "${TRAEFIK_HTTP_PORT}:80"
      - "${TRAEFIK_HTTPS_PORT}:443"
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
      - traefik_letsencrypt:/letsencrypt
    networks:
      - proxy

  db:
    image: mariadb:10.11
    container_name: nc-db
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: --transaction-isolation=READ-COMMITTED --binlog-format=ROW
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}
      MYSQL_DATABASE: ${MYSQL_DATABASE}
      MYSQL_USER: ${MYSQL_USER}
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/mysql
    networks:
      - internal

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: nc-redis
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["redis-server","--appendonly","yes"]
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    networks:
      - internal

  nextcloud:
    image: nextcloud:28-fpm-alpine
    container_name: nextcloud
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      MYSQL_HOST: db
      MYSQL_DATABASE: ${MYSQL_DATABASE}
      MYSQL_USER: ${MYSQL_USER}
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_PASSWORD}
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT: 1024M
      PHP_UPLOAD_LIMIT: 1024M
    volumes:
      - nextcloud_data:/var/www/html
      - nextcloud_apps:/var/www/html/custom_apps
      - nextcloud_config:/var/www/html/config
      - nextcloud_custom:/var/www/html/custom
      - ./provision/nextcloud-init.sh:/docker-entrypoint.d/10-nextcloud-init.sh:ro
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    networks:
      - internal

  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    container_name: nc-nginx
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - nextcloud_data:/var/www/html:ro
      - ./provision/nginx-nextcloud.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - nextcloud
    networks:
      - internal
      - proxy
    labels:
      - traefik.enable=true
      - traefik.http.routers.nc.rule=Host(`${CLOUD_DOMAIN}`)
      - traefik.http.routers.nc.entrypoints=websecure
      - traefik.http.routers.nc.tls.certresolver=le
      - traefik.http.routers.nc-secure-redirect.rule=Host(`${CLOUD_DOMAIN}`)
      - traefik.http.routers.nc-secure-redirect.entrypoints=web
      - traefik.http.routers.nc-secure-redirect.middlewares=redirect-to-https@docker
      - traefik.http.middlewares.redirect-to-https.redirectscheme.scheme=https
      - traefik.http.services.nc.loadbalancer.server.port=80

  onlyoffice:
    image: onlyoffice/documentserver:7.5
    container_name: onlyoffice
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      JWT_ENABLED: "true"
      JWT_SECRET: ${OO_JWT_SECRET}
    volumes:
      - onlyoffice_data:/var/www/onlyoffice/Data
    networks:
      - proxy
    labels:
      - traefik.enable=true
      - traefik.http.routers.oo.rule=Host(`${DOCS_DOMAIN}`)
      - traefik.http.routers.oo.entrypoints=websecure
      - traefik.http.routers.oo.tls.certresolver=le
      - traefik.http.routers.oo-redirect.rule=Host(`${DOCS_DOMAIN}`)
      - traefik.http.routers.oo-redirect.entrypoints=web
      - traefik.http.routers.oo-redirect.middlewares=redirect-to-https@docker
      - traefik.http.services.oo.loadbalancer.server.port=80

  openldap:
    image: osixia/openldap:1.5.0
    container_name: openldap
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      LDAP_ORGANISATION: "${LDAP_ORG}"
      LDAP_DOMAIN: "${LDAP_DOMAIN}"
      LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: "${LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD}"
      LDAP_READONLY_USER: "true"
      LDAP_READONLY_USER_PASSWORD: "${LDAP_READONLY_USER_PASSWORD}"
    volumes:
      - ldap_data:/var/lib/ldap
      - ldap_config:/etc/ldap/slapd.d
      - ./provision/ldap-bootstrap:/container/service/slapd/assets/config/bootstrap/ldif/custom:ro
    networks:
      - internal
      - proxy
    labels:
      - traefik.enable=false

  phpldapadmin:
    image: osixia/phpldapadmin:0.9.0
    container_name: phpldapadmin
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      PHPLDAPADMIN_LDAP_HOSTS: openldap
      PHPLDAPADMIN_HTTPS: "false"
    networks:
      - proxy
      - internal
    labels:
      - traefik.enable=true
      - traefik.http.routers.pla.rule=Host(`ldap.${CLOUD_DOMAIN}`)
      - traefik.http.routers.pla.entrypoints=websecure
      - traefik.http.routers.pla.tls.certresolver=le
      - traefik.http.routers.pla-redirect.rule=Host(`ldap.${CLOUD_DOMAIN}`)
      - traefik.http.routers.pla-redirect.entrypoints=web
      - traefik.http.routers.pla-redirect.middlewares=redirect-to-https@docker
      - traefik.http.services.pla.loadbalancer.server.port=80
{noformat}

----

h1. 3) {{provision/nginx-nextcloud.conf}}

{noformat}server {
  listen 80;
  server_name _;
  root /var/www/html;

  add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
  add_header X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN;
  add_header X-XSS-Protection "1; mode=block";

  index index.php index.html /index.php$request_uri;

  client_max_body_size 1024M;
  fastcgi_buffers 64 4k;

  location = /robots.txt { allow all; log_not_found off; access_log off; }

  location ~ ^/(?:build|tests|config|lib|3rdparty|templates|data)/ { deny all; }
  location ~ ^/(?:\.|autotest|occ|issue|indie|db_|console) { deny all; }

  location / {
    try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php$request_uri;
  }

  location ~ \.php(?:$|/) {
    fastcgi_split_path_info ^(.+?\.php)(/.*)$;
    include fastcgi_params;
    fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name;
    fastcgi_param PATH_INFO $fastcgi_path_info;
    fastcgi_param modHeadersAvailable true;
    fastcgi_param front_controller_active true;
    fastcgi_pass nextcloud:9000;
    fastcgi_intercept_errors on;
    fastcgi_request_buffering off;
  }

  location ~ \.(?:css|js|woff2?|svg|gif|map)$ {
    try_files $uri /index.php$request_uri;
    expires 6M;
    access_log off;
  }

  location ~ \.(?:png|html|ttf|ico|jpg|jpeg)$ {
    try_files $uri /index.php$request_uri;
    expires 6M;
    access_log off;
  }
}
{noformat}

----

h1. 5) Nextcloud Provisioner: {{provision/nextcloud-init.sh}}

{noformat}#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "[nc-init] Waiting for DB..."
until php -r "try { new PDO('mysql:host='.getenv('MYSQL_HOST').';dbname='.getenv('MYSQL_DATABASE'), getenv('MYSQL_USER'), getenv('MYSQL_PASSWORD')); echo 'ok'; } catch (Exception \$e) { exit(1);}"; do
  sleep 2
done

NC_PATH="/var/www/html"
cd "$NC_PATH"

if [ ! -f "$NC_PATH/config/config.php" ]; then
  echo "[nc-init] Installing Nextcloud..."
  php occ maintenance:install \
    --database "mysql" \
    --database-host "$MYSQL_HOST" \
    --database-name "$MYSQL_DATABASE" \
    --database-user "$MYSQL_USER" \
    --database-pass "$MYSQL_PASSWORD" \
    --admin-user "${NC_ADMIN_USER:-admin}" \
    --admin-pass "${NC_ADMIN_PASS:-adminpass}"

  php occ config:system:set trusted_domains 0 --value="${CLOUD_DOMAIN:-cloud.local}"
  php occ config:system:set overwrite.cli.url --value="https://${CLOUD_DOMAIN:-cloud.local}"
  php occ config:system:set default_phone_region --value="IN"
  php occ config:system:set memcache.local --value="\\OC\\Memcache\\APCu"
  php occ config:system:set memcache.locking --value="\\OC\\Memcache\\Redis"
  php occ config:system:set redis host --value="redis"
  php occ config:system:set redis port --value="6379"
fi

echo "[nc-init] Enabling core apps..."
php occ app:enable user_ldap || true
php occ app:enable workflowengine || true
php occ app:enable files_automatedtagging || true
php occ app:enable systemtags || true
php occ app:enable approval || true
php occ app:enable onlyoffice || true

echo "[nc-init] Configure ONLYOFFICE..."
php occ config:app:set onlyoffice DocumentServerUrl --value="https://${DOCS_DOMAIN:-docs.local}/"
php occ config:app:set onlyoffice DocumentServerJwtSecret --value="${OO_JWT_SECRET:-change-me}"
php occ config:app:set onlyoffice jwt_secret --value="${OO_JWT_SECRET:-change-me}"

echo "[nc-init] Configure LDAP (base settings, adjust filters as needed)..."
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapHost "openldap"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapBase "${LDAP_BASE_DN:-dc=example,dc=com}"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapAgentName "cn=admin,${LDAP_BASE_DN:-dc=example,dc=com}"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapAgentPassword "${LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin}"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapTLS "0"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapPort "389"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapUserFilter "(|(objectClass=inetOrgPerson)(objectClass=person))"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapGroupFilter "(objectClass=posixGroup)"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapLoginFilter "(&(objectClass=inetOrgPerson)(uid=%uid))"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapUserDisplayName "cn"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapUserFilterMode "1"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 ldapGroupDisplayName "cn"
php occ ldap:set-config s01 turnOnPasswordChange "0"
php occ ldap:test-config s01 || true
php occ ldap:show-config

echo "[nc-init] Create ISO control tags..."
php occ system:tag:create "Draft" || true
php occ system:tag:create "In Review" || true
php occ system:tag:create "Approved" || true
php occ system:tag:create "Obsolete" || true

# Save tag IDs for later (best-effort)
DRAFT_ID=$(php occ system:tag:list | awk '/\bDraft\b/ {print $1; exit}')
INREVIEW_ID=$(php occ system:tag:list | awk '/\bIn Review\b/ {print $1; exit}')
APPROVED_ID=$(php occ system:tag:list | awk '/\bApproved\b/ {print $1; exit}')
OBSOLETE_ID=$(php occ system:tag:list | awk '/\bObsolete\b/ {print $1; exit}')
echo "[nc-init] Tag IDs: Draft=${DRAFT_ID} InReview=${INREVIEW_ID} Approved=${APPROVED_ID} Obsolete=${OBSOLETE_ID}"

echo "[nc-init] Seed ISO folders (optional)..."
php occ files:scan --all || true

cat <<'NOTE'

[nc-init] ========= NEXT STEPS (once containers are up) =========
1) Ensure DNS points to:
   - ${CLOUD_DOMAIN}  -> Traefik server
   - ${DOCS_DOMAIN}   -> Traefik server
   - ldap.${CLOUD_DOMAIN} -> Traefik server

2) Login to Nextcloud as ${NC_ADMIN_USER} / ${NC_ADMIN_PASS}

3) Approvals & Flow:
   - Approval app is enabled. In Files, select a document -> "Approval" sidebar.
   - Create a simple approval workflow:
       * In Settings -> Flow, add rule:
         WHEN file is tagged "In Review"
         THEN send approval request to group "Approvers"
         (and on approve -> add tag "Approved"; on reject -> add tag "Draft")
     (CLI creation of Flow rules is limited; the above tags/groups are pre-created.)

4) LDAP:
   - Add users via phpLDAPadmin at https://ldap.${CLOUD_DOMAIN}
   - Put users into groups: Editors / Reviewers / Approvers / ComplianceAdmins
   - In Nextcloud -> LDAP/AD Integration, click "Detect Base DN" and "Test". The base config is already applied.

5) ONLYOFFICE:
   - In Nextcloud -> Settings -> ONLYOFFICE, verify:
       Document Server: https://${DOCS_DOMAIN}
       JWT Secret: set (matches compose)

6) Security hardening:
   - Set strong passwords & rotate ${OO_JWT_SECRET}.
   - Restrict Traefik dashboard (currently off).
   - Consider enabling 2FA in Nextcloud.

==============================================================
NOTE
{noformat}

{quote}*Why a small manual step for Flow?* Nextcloud’s Flow/Approval rules do not (yet) have stable, documented OCC commands for creating arbitrary rule chains. The script pre-creates *tags* and *apps* so you can finish the rule in the UI in under a minute. If you prefer, I can provide a small *headless browser* or *OCS API* example to auto-click that in CI.{quote}

----

h2. How the ISO Document Control Flow works (recommended pattern)

* *Author (Editors group)* creates/edits document → tag *Draft*.
* When ready, Editor switches tag to *In Review*.
* *Flow rule* triggers *Approval request* to *Reviewers* or *Approvers* group.
* If *approved* → tag *Approved* (and optionally move to a read-only folder).
* If *rejected* → tag *Draft* with a comment.
* When superseded → tag *Obsolete* and move to archive.

This mirrors ISO 9001/27001 doc control and gives you clean auditability (tags + versions + OnlyOffice change tracking).

----

h2. Running it

# Create folders and files shown above, then:

{noformat}docker compose --env-file .env up -d
{noformat}

# Ensure your DNS records for {{${CLOUD_DOMAIN}}}, {{${DOCS_DOMAIN}}}, and {{ldap.${CLOUD_DOMAIN}}} point to this host. Traefik will auto-issue Let’s Encrypt certs.

----

h2. Optional hardening / addons

* *Fail2ban* / *CrowdSec* in front of Traefik
* *Nextcloud full-text search* (Elasticsearch) if needed
* *Group Folders* app for departmental permissions
* *Audit app* in Nextcloud for extended logs

h1. *Document Version Control & Approval System – Overview*

h2. ✅ *Purpose*

As part of our *ISO* and *SOC 2* compliance requirements, we need:

* Controlled document management
* Proper versioning with audit history
* Approval workflows (Draft → Review → Approved → Obsolete)
* Centralized, secure access for all employees

We have implemented a *self-hosted, secure, web-based document management system* that meets these requirements while remaining *easy to use for non-technical staff*.

----

h2. ✅ *What This System Includes*

* *Nextcloud*: Central platform for storing and sharing documents.
* *ONLYOFFICE*: Online editing for Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files in your browser.
* *Version Control*: Every document edit creates a new version, allowing rollback.
* *Approval Workflow*:
** *Draft* → *In Review* → *Approved* → *Obsolete*
** Automated notifications to approvers.
* *Access Control via LDAP*:
** Users and groups are managed centrally.
** Groups: *Editors*, *Reviewers*, *Approvers*, *ComplianceAdmins*.
* *Audit-Ready Logs*:
** Who edited what, when.
** Who approved or rejected changes.
* *Secure Access*:
** SSL encryption (HTTPS).
** Role-based permissions.
** Can integrate 2FA.

----

h2. ✅ *How Users Will Use the System*

h3. *For All Users*

* *Access the portal*: {{https://<company-cloud-domain>}}
* *Login with your company credentials* (same as LDAP/AD username).
* *Browse documents* in folders by department or category.
* *Download or view* documents online.

----

h3. *For Editors (Document Authors)*

# *Create or upload a document* in the appropriate folder.
# Edit directly in your browser using *ONLYOFFICE* (no need to download MS Office).
# Tag the document as *Draft* while working on it.
# When ready for review, change the tag to *In Review*.
#* This automatically *notifies reviewers/approvers*.

----

h3. *For Reviewers / Approvers*

# You’ll receive a *notification* when a document needs review.
# Open the document in the portal:
#* Review contents directly in the browser.
#* Use comments or track changes if needed.
# Use the *Approval sidebar* to:
#* *Approve* (document moves to “Approved” state).
#* *Reject* (document goes back to “Draft”).
# When a document is updated in the future, the cycle repeats.

----

h3. *For Compliance / Management*

* *Dashboards and audit logs* show:
** Which documents are pending review.
** Who approved which document and when.
** Complete version history for every file.
* *Obsolete documents* can be archived with an “Obsolete” tag.
* Reports can be exported for *ISO audits*.

----

h2. ✅ *Advantages of This System*

h3. *For Management*

* Full *compliance with ISO & SOC2 requirements* for document control.
* *Audit-ready* history of approvals, edits, and user activity.
* *Centralized control* – no more scattered versions across emails and desktops.
* *Cost-efficient* – built entirely on *open-source, self-hosted tools* (no recurring license fees).

h3. *For End Users*

* *Familiar experience*: Works like a shared drive but with *modern web features*.
* *No special software required* – just a browser.
* *Edit Office documents online* (Word, Excel, PowerPoint).
* *Automatic versioning* – no need to save “v1, v2, final-final.docx”.
* *Clear approval process* – no confusion over which document is the latest.

h3. *For IT & Security*

* *Self-hosted* → data stays within company premises.
* *Secure access control* via company LDAP/AD.
* *Encrypted communication* (HTTPS).
* Easy to *backup and restore*.

----

h2. ✅ *Typical Document Lifecycle*

# *Create* → Tagged as *Draft*.
# *Submit for Review* → Tag changed to *In Review*.
# *Approval Process*:
#* *Approve* → Tag = Approved (read-only for most users).
#* *Reject* → Tag = Draft (returns to author).
# *Periodic Review*:
#* If obsolete → Tag = Obsolete (archived).
# *Audit Trail*:
#* Every step recorded for compliance.

----

h2. ✅ *FAQs*

*Q: Do I need MS Office installed?*
No. All editing happens in your browser using ONLYOFFICE.

*Q: Can I restore an old version?*
Yes. Every edit is versioned and can be restored.

*Q: Who sees my drafts?*
Only your team or assigned group, based on permissions.
